entities.name: James of Baux
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
James of Baux (or James of Les Baux) emerged as a pivotal, albeit ultimately unsuccessful, figure in the twilight of the Latin Empire of Constantinople, holding the titular imperial claim from 1374 until his death on July 17, 1383. A scion of the powerful Baux family from Provence, his claim to the Latin imperial throne derived from his mother, Margaret of Taranto, who was the daughter of Philip I, Prince of Taranto and Emperor of Constantinople. His reign marked the definitive end of any practical territorial control for the Latin emperors, as the Byzantine Palaiologos dynasty had largely re-established control over the city decades prior, leaving James to rule over scattered feudal remnants and an increasingly abstract imperial ideal. His tenure reflects the fragmented political landscape of the late medieval Mediterranean, caught between Western crusading ambitions and the growing Ottoman threat.

James's claim to the Latin Empire was asserted following the death of his uncle, Philip II, Prince of Taranto, in 1373. He inherited not a functioning empire, but rather the rights to the Principality of Achaea and the suzerainty over the Duchy of Athens, along with the prestigious but largely empty imperial title. His effective rule was primarily limited to Achaea in the Peloponnese, where he struggled to maintain authority against local Frankish barons and the encroaching Navarrese Company, a mercenary force that seized significant portions of the principality in 1378. Despite his grand title, James's actual power dwindled, forcing him to mortgage his rights to Achaea to the Knights Hospitaller for five years in 1376 in exchange for a substantial sum of 12,000 ducats, a clear indication of his financial and political distress.
